full_judgment:
"13. It had been held in a number of decisions that the Artha Rin Adalat is not an ordinary Civil Court but a special forum of limited jurisdiction. The question, therefore, arises whether an order passed by a Court of Special jurisdiction is revisable by this Court under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. We can resolve this question, easily if we can find the answer to the question, is the Artha Rin Adalat a Court subordinate to the High Court Division. In deciding this issue with regard to the special status the superior Courts of this sub-continent have formulated certain principles. If appeal lies from a Special Tribunal to the High Court then that Special Tribunal is subordinate to the High Court. Similarly, if the Special Court is under the administrative control of the High Court it is also subordinate to the High Court. If we examine the provisions of the Act we find that an appeal shall lie against a judgment and decree of the Artha Rin Adalat to the High Court Division. Section 4(2) of the Act provides that the Judges of the Artha Rin Adalat will be appointed from amongst the Subordinate Judges with consultation with the Supreme Court. Rule framed under the Act provides that the Artha Rin Adalat will be under the administrative control of the Supreme Court. It has been held in one case that if the court is one from which an appeal lies to the High Court though in certain specified case, then the Court is subject to the appellate jurisdiction of the High Court and that is sufficient to attract the power of superintendency conferred on the High Court. Besides Article 109 of the Constitution provides that the High Court Division shall have superintendence and control over all Courts subordinate to it and Article 114 provides that there shall be in addition to the Supreme Court such Courts subordinate thereto as may be established by Law". 

 9. We have gone through these decisions of our High Court Division and it appears that the decisions were given in the same line holding that when appeal lies before the High Court Division against any decree and judgment passed by the Artha Rin Adalat it is subordinate to the High Court Division and is under the control and superintendence  of this Division and, as such, it is a Civil Court and so section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure can be  invoked against any order passed by the Artha Rin  Adalat. It may be pointed out that 48 DLR 57 decision was given by the Division Bench on 25th July, 1994 and in BLT case the same was delivered on 20th March, 1995. 

 "22. Revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division is provided for in section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and in making under section 6 the proceeding, order, judgment and decree of an Artha Rin Adalat not amenable to interference by any Court or authority, the aim of the Adalat Act was to create departures from the Code of Civil Procedure. Section 7, it may be said, was meant to be an exception to this complete ouster of interference. An exception has been made in respect of a judgment and decree in section 7(1). Another exception has been made in respect of a final order under Order 9, rule 13 CPC. In both cases appeal will be to the High Court Division. There is room for argument that both the appellate, revisional powers of interference with any order interlocutory or otherwise, is expressly barred by section 6. The proviso to section 7(1) barring an appeal against an interlocutory order has been provided for only as a measure of abundant caution. In other words, section 6 is the master ouster provision, section 7 is an exception to that ouster. The exception cannot render the ouster provision nugatory". 

 11. The aforesaid findings clearly indicate that any order passed by the Artha Rin Adalat is not amenable to the jurisdiction of this Division under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure as there is express bar in section 6 which is the master ouster of jurisdiction. Before the Appellate Division it was argued that proviso to section 7 indicate that no appeal shall lie against interlocutory order of the Adalat, which means the appeal is barred but a revision shall lie before the High Court Division in respect of both the appealable and revisional orders. The Appellate Division disposed of this in the aforesaid manner in paragraph No.22 of the decision. In section 6 of the Ain it has been provided that no order of an Artha Rin Adalat is amenable to interference by any Court or authority, the only exception is section 7 where a provision for appeal has been made in respect of any judgment and decree or an order passed under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Admittedly, the Artha Rin Adalat Ain is a special forum set up under a special legislation and the remedies will follow as provided in the Ain itself and it has been indicated by our Appellate Division that if there is any exclusion indicated in the Ain, as in section 6, it will include a remedy under the general law. So, on going through this decision of the Appellate Division, we hold that there is a complete ouster of jurisdiction of the High Court Division for interference under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against any interlocutory matter or orders passed by the Adalat. In the two High Court Division decisions as aforesaid, this decision of our Appellate Division has not been looked into considered. We on perusal of this decision of our Appellate Division, are of the view that the impugned order is not revisable under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure as there is total bar under the Ain. 

 14. This indicates that only the financial institutions may institute suit in the Adalat for realisation of any advance made to any party as a loan. Here in the present case admittedly the plaintiff is not a financial institution as contemplated under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain and, as such, they have no right to institute the suit in the Adalat and the Adalat has no jurisdiction to entertain such a suit. The suit if otherwise maintainable may be instituted in any other appropriate forum but not before the Artha Rin Adalat. The precondition for filing the suit before the Artha Rin Adalat is that it must be a financial institution as contemplated under section 2 of the Ain which is very much absent in the case of present plaintiff-opposite party No. 1. So, the institution and continuation of the suit before the Adalat is illegal and beyond jurisdiction. It appears that, taking this ground that as the plaintiff is not a financial institution the filing and entertainment of the suit in the Artha Rin Adalat is illegal the present petitioner filed a petition under Order 7, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure for return of the plaint which was rejected by the trial Court on the ground that the plaintiff is a society which advanced the money to the present petitioner and that the Court also disposed of certain other suits of similar nature. But to attract jurisdiction of the Adalat it must follow the provision of section 2 of the Ain. It must first examine whether the plaintiff is a financial institution and that the amount involved is a loan without which no suit can be entertained by the Adalat. Here in the present case admittedly the plaintiff is not a financial institution as contemplated under section 2 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, But the suit has been entertained by the Adalat. It is well-settled that Artha Rin Adalat Ain is a self contained Code and the Adalat is not a Civil Court having all the powers of the Code of Civil Procedure. It is a Civil Court of defined nature and jurisdiction. This Adalat can entertain only those suits as contemplated under the Ain Now if a suit is filed by an authority, which is not a financial institution, can it be allowed to proceed further? In the Ain no provision has been made for return or rejection of the plaint as contemplated under Order 7, rules 10 and 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In such a situation can the aggrieved party be left without any relief. We have considered this aspect of the matter and the observation of our Appellate Division in 14 BLD cases and we are of the view that the Court is not left without power and the party is not left without any relief. When it is apparent on the face of the record that the suit has been wrongly entertained and proceeded with in the Adalat, this Court may act under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It provided that nothing in this Code shall be deemed to limit or otherwise affect the inherent power of the Court to make such orders as may be necessary for the ends of justice or to prevent abuse of the process of the Court. The continuation of the suit before the Artha Rin Adalat is an abuse of the process of the Court as any decree passed by the Adalat in such a suit will be without jurisdiction and, as such, a nullity. As that has been filed under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure it is not maintainable against an order passed by the Artha Rin Adalat, we are inclined to act under section 151(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and make the Rule absolute with a-direction to the Adalat to return the plaint to the filing Advocate for presentation before the proper Court.
